name: Berberism
summary: Berberism (Amazigh activism) is the North African movement for recognition of Berber identity, history and languages, chiefly in Morocco and Algeria. Its core demands are official status and schooling for Tamazight, an end to Arabisation, a rewritten national history and development of marginalised Berber regions. In Algeria the Kabyle strand also pressed for pluralist democracy and secularism against single-party and Islamist politics, while the Moroccan strand has mostly worked within the monarchy.
scope: The mainstream cultural, linguistic and democratic Amazigh rights movement since the late 1960s: Mouloud Mammeri's circle, the 1980 Berber Spring and the Kabyle MCB, RCD and FFS tradition in Algeria, and Morocco's Agadir Charter (1991) and Amazigh Manifesto (2000). It excludes the separatist MAK wing, Canarian Berber-symbol nationalism, and Tuareg politics.

sources.title: Charte d'Agadir relative aux droits linguistiques et culturels (1991)
sources.author: Moroccan Amazigh associations
sources.usedFor: Pluralist Moroccan identity, critique of the centralised unitary state, and demands for constitutional recognition, schooling, media and research.

sources.title: Manifeste berbère (2000)
sources.author: Amazigh signatories, Morocco
sources.usedFor: Nine demands: official status, teaching, history rewrite, regional development, media, names, and a brotherhood framing of Amazighs and Arabs.

sources.title: Amazigh Politics in the Wake of the Arab Spring
sources.author: Bruce Maddy-Weitzman (University of Texas Press, 2022)
sources.usedFor: Scholarly account of the Berber/Amazigh movement: Berber Spring, Agadir Charter, Berber Manifesto, FFS and RCD, relations with Islamism and the state.

notes: Searched the Charter, the Manifesto and both books for each theme; economic, ecological, religious-law and foreign-policy questions are not addressed by these sources. Kabyle secularism and the one-party critique are documented for individuals and parties (Aïtel on Matoub and Djaout; Maddy-Weitzman on the RCD and MAK), not as stated tenets of the mainstream movement, so those statements stay null.
